narrative:
The model estimated a 61.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is above the threshold used for admission, your law school application was denied: the prediction says failure is more likely than passing, not that failure is certain.

The largest reason for that outcome was your third-year class standing. You are in the lowest decile in your school, compared with accepted students who average around the sixth decile. This was the strongest factor and it pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your LSAT score of 35, below the accepted average of 37.18, and your undergraduate GPA of 2.90, below the accepted average of 3.23, were the next most important factors, but in this case both exerted a modest pull toward passing rather than failure. Even so, they were not enough to offset the much stronger concern about your third-year academic rank.

To improve a future application, focus on the clearest area of concern: seek academic advising and take steps to strengthen your record, especially your upper-year performance. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve your score, and ask admissions staff what additional evidence or context they would accept. A later application with stronger indicators and a clear improvement plan would give the model and reviewers a better case for admission.
